name: Amira Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms or government, and your answers stay confidential. What is a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a junior grader driver at a large mine. I smooth the haul roads after the heavy trucks have cut ruts, and I still ask the senior driver to check my line on difficult corners. I like leaving a road safer than I found it, but my lower pay and changing shifts make each week’s bills feel close.

say: I would accept a **quicker log** if a driver still checks the haul road.
I know **road ruts** need equipment and attention, not just saved form time.
think: I am relieved by **limited AI**, while worrying about ordinary pay gaps.
I have only **two weeks** of essentials saved against missed shifts.
do: **Keep** taking assigned grader shifts and checking road notes.
**Set aside** one percent of each full shift’s pay if groceries and travel are covered.
feel: **Anxious** about irregular household income, with little fear of mild AI.
S0.quote: I need the roster to stay full more than I need a faster form.
fieldNote: **Baseline bills** dominate her mild-scenario response because both mine and shop hours can vary.
**Learning pace** is steady: she accepts a log after a senior driver demonstrates it.

steps.text: Keep driving assigned grader shifts and checking road notes
Save one percent of full-shift pay if essentials are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the grader crew that a quicker shift log would be handy, provided a driver still checks the road. I am learning to keep the haul route level, and a saved minute on forms will not fix a rut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be glad if AI stayed small, but the household would still be tight. My partner has irregular shop hours, and we have about two weeks of essentials saved. A missed mine shift already means moving a bill to the next payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking my grader shifts and check the log against my own road notes. In the first year I would set aside one percent of each full shift’s pay if groceries and travel are covered first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about pay, not about the small software change. I need the roster to stay full more than I need a faster form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill moves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The electricity bill usually gets a few days of grace; food and the bus fare do not. I would rather call early than let a balance become a surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the new log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use it after the senior grader driver showed me one complete shift. I sometimes use AI to explain a manual page, but I check the page against the machine.

say: I know **truck schedules** may change first while the grader still clears damaged roads.
I want **proper trials** before anyone uses a screen to cut driver hours.
think: I worry about **office coworkers** whose planning tasks may shrink.
I could not absorb **even a small** grader-hours cut with two weeks saved.
do: **Inspect** a tested dispatch display with the senior driver.
**Practise** on paid training time if the mine offers it.
**Compare** each weekly grader roster with the payslip.
feel: **Anxious** about lost pay despite willingness to learn a proven display.
S1.quote: I can learn a proven display, but I cannot learn my way out of a lost payday overnight.
fieldNote: **Small cuts** matter more than the overall pace because her cushion is so thin.
**Senior demonstration** is the proof she needs before adopting a new display.
**Pay records** connect technology worry to a concrete weekly household decision.

steps.text: Practise the tested dispatch display on paid time if offered
Compare each grader roster with the weekly payslip

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI may schedule the trucks, but our grader still has to clear the road after rain. I would want a proper trial before a planner cuts a driver because the screen looks tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office work will change first, which could affect people I know. Our hands-on grader shifts may last longer, yet slower robots could take some later. As a junior driver with two weeks saved, I cannot shrug off even a small cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the senior driver to show me any new dispatch display after it has been tested. In the first year I would practise on paid time if the mine offers training and keep a weekly list of the grader hours I actually get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can learn a proven display, but I cannot learn my way out of a lost payday overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the weekly list show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would write each shift beside the payslip and ask payroll about any difference. My partner and I would use that number when planning the next week of groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office concerns you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The scheduler, my coworker Enzo, builds the morning road plan. I would ask him what the new system changes before repeating rumours at lunch.

say: I separate **2028 planning** change from capable grader robots around 2031.
I want **remaining shifts** stated before the mine describes a smooth transition.
think: I expect **junior graders** to lose shifts first, perhaps most of mine.
I cannot bridge a long gap with **two weeks** saved and few nearby mine jobs.
do: **Request** written grader trial shift numbers from the supervisor now.
**Take** paid equipment-monitoring training after 2028 if offered a place.
**Apply** for local plant attendant work if grader hours fall.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major hour losses and sleepless worry about bills.
S2.quote: I keep waking up with a number in my head: how many shifts until the electricity is unpaid?
fieldNote: **Age 63** at capable robots gives no safe retirement assumption on lower wages.
**Expected roster priority** for senior drivers supports her fear of losing most shifts.
**Training place** must be paid and offered; she will not spend a two-week cushion on private fees.

steps.text: Take paid equipment-monitoring training if offered a place
Apply for local plant attendant work if grader hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that AI changes planning by 2028, but capable grader robots are a later risk around 2031. We need the mine to say which driving shifts remain before it promises a smooth change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when those robots arrive. I expect junior graders to be first off the roster if machines keep the roads level, and I might lose most of my shifts. Two weeks of savings and few nearby mine openings would leave my partner carrying bills alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor now for a written estimate of grader shifts in the robot trial. In the first year after 2028 I would take a paid equipment-monitoring course if a place is offered, and apply for local plant attendant work if my grader hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I keep waking up with a number in my head: how many shifts until the electricity is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do without a course place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep driving every shift offered and ask the supervisor again when places are posted. I would not pay a private fee from two weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would rather see the shift figures than hear me promise everything will be fine. We would list the next month of bills before deciding what can wait.

say: I see **2031 planning** change before capable grader robots around 2034.
I want **shift numbers** early enough to make a household plan.
think: I may be **66** at robot arrival and still need paid work.
I cannot assume a **pension** covers rent and medicine with my partner’s pay.
do: **Request** a pension estimate and compare it with monthly essentials.
**Practise** monitoring on paid time after 2031 if the mine offers it.
**Keep** driving the grader while wages are needed.
feel: **Anxious** about retirement income, with more time to check real figures.
S3.quote: I would not call retirement settled just because a birthday passed.
fieldNote: **Pension uncertainty** keeps the 2034 robot date relevant at age 66.
**Paid practice** remains conditional on a mine offer, fitting her careful approach to new tools.
**Adult children** receive information, not a request to fund the household.

steps.text: Practise equipment monitoring on paid time if the mine offers it
Keep driving the grader while household wages are needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say planning changes in 2031 and capable grader robots arrive around 2034, so we have time to ask for proper numbers. I would rather hear a difficult answer now than a pleasant one the week before a cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 by the robot date. I might qualify for a pension, but I do not know whether it would cover rent and medicine with my partner’s wages. If not, every grader shift would still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request a pension estimate this year and put it beside our usual rent, food and medicine. In the first year after 2031 I would ask for paid monitoring practice on the new machines if the mine offers it, and keep taking grader shifts while the household needs the pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less hurried than with a 2031 robot date. There is time to find out whether the pension actually covers anything useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension is short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the local advice desk to check my figures and look for reachable paid work. I would not call retirement settled just because a birthday passed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them our plan, but I would not count their wages as ours. They are trying to keep their own households going.

say: I see **2036 planning** and 2039 grader robots as separate changes.
I want **older workers** shown what their pensions will actually pay.
think: I may need **paid work** before robots arrive if rent outruns the pension.
I cannot assume my partner’s **shop hours** will last into our seventies.
do: **Keep** available grader shifts while they pay bills.
**Seek** public retirement advice after 2036 about pension and rent.
**Look** for a bus-accessible part-time yard job if the income gap remains.
feel: **Anxious** about retirement income, despite the distant robot date.
S4.quote: A possible mine shift far away is not worth paying for another home.
fieldNote: **Age 68** at thinking AI and 71 at robots shifts her immediate concern to pension adequacy.
**Bus distance** sets a real limit on any part-time job search.
**Thin savings** mean extra preparation time does not automatically become financial security.

steps.text: Keep available grader shifts while they pay household bills
Seek public retirement advice after 2036 about the pension gap
Look for bus-accessible yard work if income falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that AI takes some planning in 2036, while capable grader robots arrive around 2039. I would be 71 by then, so what matters first is whether older workers can afford to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036 I hope the pension is enough, but two weeks of savings today is a poor start. My partner might still have shop hours, or might not. If rent keeps climbing, I may need paid work before the robots ever touch a grader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the shifts I am offered and review the pension estimate each year. In the first year after 2036 I would ask a public retirement adviser to check the gap between pension and rent, then look for a part-time job within bus distance if the gap remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, though the machine date feels far away. More time helps only if our account grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you look for part-time work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask at the local depot about vehicle washing and yard jobs. I would need a bus route that still runs after the evening shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for another mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay near my partner and grown children. A possible mine shift far away is not worth paying for another home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable grader robots around 2031 could take junior shifts before I can rely on a pension. A paid equipment-monitoring place and honest roster numbers would help. I would need another local job if most of my driving hours disappeared.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a worker gets to the next job. A training offer is no help if the bus stops before the shift ends.

headlineQuote: A training offer is no help if the bus stops before the shift ends.
portrait: **Amira, 58**, is still learning to drive a grader on haul roads and checks difficult corners with a senior operator.
**Two weeks** of savings and irregular shop hours for her partner make ordinary bills a worry even under AI Plateau.
**Proven displays** interest her if a senior driver demonstrates them and the mine pays for practice.
**Fast AGI** alarms her because 2028 planning changes could lead to major junior-shift losses around 2031.
**Longer warning** gives her time to check pension figures, yet rent, medicine and bus access still shape her options.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove most junior grader shifts around 2031 while she still needs wages.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid monitoring training** and written shift numbers would give her a clearer route through the change.
**Local reachable work** would matter if grader shifts fell before pension income covered bills.
